html:
A Sanskrit textbook of arithmetic and measurement written in 1150 by the Indian mathematician Bhaskara II. It is the first part of his larger work on mathematics and astronomy, the Siddhanta Shiromani.

It is written in verse, and many problems are addressed to a girl called Lilavati, "the playful one". A later story says she was Bhaskara's daughter, whose wedding hour was spoiled when a pearl fell into the water clock; the book was his consolation to her. Whether true or not, the charm helped make it the most popular mathematics text in India for centuries.

It covers the place-value numbers and zero, fractions, interest, the rule of three, series, permutations and combinations, areas and volumes. Problems are set in daily life: bees and lotus flowers, merchants and their profits. Bhaskara built on Brahmagupta and others, and his work fed the later Kerala school. In 1587 the poet Faizi translated the Lilavati into Persian for Akbar.
sum: A Sanskrit textbook of arithmetic and measurement written in 1150 by the Indian mathematician Bhaskara II. It is the first part of his larger work on mathematics and astronomy, the Siddhanta Shiromani.
